lead: A running program has three open channels: one for input, one for normal results, one for error messages. The shell numbers them 0, 1 and 2 and can point any of them at a file instead of the terminal, before the program starts. That is what file input and output means in a script: the script still reads stdin and writes stdout, but the shell has already swapped the destination. Nightly backups, cron jobs and log-writing scripts all rest on this one idea.
prereq: You need: 3.1 Shell basics, 3.2 Shell variables and operators for quoting, 3.3 Conditionals and loops for while, and the Unit 2 notes on file permissions to know who may read the file.

sections.h3: Standard input, standard output, standard error

blocks.text: Every process starts with three open channels called file descriptors. A file descriptor is a small whole number the kernel uses to name an open file. Number 0 is standard input, or stdin: the stream that read and cat take text from. Number 1 is standard output, or stdout: where echo and printf write results. Number 2 is standard error, or stderr: where error messages go. By default all three are attached to your terminal.

Why keep output and errors apart? Stdout carries data, clean lines that a program or a person will use later. Stderr carries complaints about the run. If both shared one channel, a line like cannot open file would sit inside your clean result. Separating them lets you save data in one file and warnings in another.

Redirection is done by the shell, not by the program. The program never learns a file name; it just writes to fd 1. So ls > list.txt works for every command, including ones written decades before you were born.

sections.h3: Redirection: pointing a descriptor at a file

items: cmd > file sends fd 1 to file. The shell creates the file, or empties it if it already exists, before cmd runs.
cmd 2> file moves only the error stream; stdout still reaches the terminal.
cmd &> file (Bash) sends both streams to the same file.
2>&1 means point fd 2 at wherever fd 1 points right now. It is an instruction about order, not a file name.

blocks.text: Order decides the result. ./run.sh > out.txt 2>&1 puts everything in out.txt, because fd 1 moves first and fd 2 then copies it. ./run.sh 2>&1 > out.txt first points fd 2 at the terminal, then moves fd 1 to the file, so errors still appear on screen.
/dev/null is a device that discards whatever is written to it and returns end of file on read. find / -name "*.conf" 2> /dev/null hides permission errors while you keep the real matches.
Several redirections can sit on one command line. ./count.sh < data.txt > out.txt 2> err.txt gives the script a file as input, a file for results and a third file for errors, all at once.

sections.h3: Reading a file line by line

blocks.text: read takes one line from stdin and cuts it into fields using IFS, the internal field separator. IFS is an ordinary shell variable holding the characters treated as separators; by default these are space, tab and newline.
In read -r a b, the first field goes to a and the rest of the line goes to b. The -r means raw: a backslash stays a backslash instead of escaping the next character.

The standard loop is while IFS= read -r line; do ...; done < file. Writing IFS= sets IFS to empty for that one command, so leading and trailing spaces survive. The < file after done attaches the file to stdin for the whole loop, so the file is opened once and read forward.
Avoid for line in $(cat file). Command substitution splits on spaces, so a name like Ravi Kumar becomes two items, a blank line vanishes, and the whole file is loaded into memory first.

A here-document feeds lines to stdin without a file. cat <, the lines, then EOF on its own line. Variables expand inside it; quote the marker as <<'EOF' to keep text literal. It is handy for writing a config file or feeding SQL to a client.

tee copies a stream: cmd | tee log.txt shows the output and saves the same bytes in log.txt. At end of file read returns a non-zero status, which simply stops the while loop. That is normal, not a failure.

spec.aria: data.txt with lines 1 2, 3 4 and 5 6 feeds fd 0 into count.sh; fd 1 goes to out.txt holding 3, 7 and 11; a dashed fd 2 goes to an empty err.txt.

examples.question: A script count.sh contains only the loop body while read -r a b; do echo $((a + b)); done. It is run as ./count.sh < data.txt > out.txt 2> err.txt. The file data.txt holds exactly three lines: "1 2", "3 4" and "5 6". State the contents of out.txt, the contents of err.txt and the exit status of the script.
steps: Before the script runs, the shell opens data.txt as fd 0, creates out.txt as fd 1 and creates err.txt as fd 2. No command in the script names a file.
Pass 1: read takes the line "1 2" and splits it on the space, so a = 1 and b = 2. $((1 + 2)) = 3, and echo writes 3 plus a newline to fd 1, which is out.txt.
Pass 2: a = 3, b = 4, so $((3 + 4)) = 7 goes to out.txt.
Pass 3: a = 5, b = 6, so $((5 + 6)) = 11 goes to out.txt.
Pass 4: read finds no characters left, returns a non-zero status, and the while loop ends. Nothing failed, so nothing is written to fd 2.
The script's exit status is the status of its last command, the loop, which ended normally: 0.
examples.answer: out.txt holds 3, 7 and 11 on three separate lines (7 bytes), err.txt is empty (0 bytes), and the exit status is 0.
examples.check:
pairs = [(1, 2), (3, 4), (5, 6)]
sums = [a + b for a, b in pairs]
for s in sums:
    print(s)
print(0)
print(len(b''.join(str(s).encode() + b'\n' for s in sums)))

traps: > empties the target before the command starts, so sort marks.txt > marks.txt leaves an empty file. Write to a second file, then move it.
2>&1 copies where fd 1 points at that moment. Putting it before > out.txt sends errors to the terminal, not to the file.
Without -r, read treats a backslash as an escape and silently drops it, so Windows-style paths change when read.
A failing read at end of file is how the loop stops. Do not test it as an error and do not print a message for it.
done < file opens the file once for the whole loop; writing read -r line < file inside the body reopens and restarts the file every pass, giving an endless loop.

quiz.q: Name the three standard file descriptors and their numbers.
quiz.a: fd 0 is standard input (stdin), fd 1 is standard output (stdout), fd 2 is standard error (stderr).

quiz.q: Why does the shell keep stdout and stderr on separate descriptors?
quiz.a: Stdout carries the data the user or the next program wants; stderr carries messages about the run. Separating them keeps error text out of a saved data file and lets each stream be redirected independently.

quiz.q: Write one command line that runs ./backup.sh and saves both its normal output and its errors in backup.log, discarding nothing.
quiz.a: ./backup.sh > backup.log 2>&1 . fd 1 moves to backup.log first, then fd 2 is copied from fd 1, so both streams end in the file.

quiz.q: What does while IFS= read -r name; do echo "[$name]"; done < guests.txt print for a line " Anil "?
quiz.a: IFS= stops trimming, so the leading and trailing spaces survive: [  Anil  ].

quiz.q: Why does grep root /etc/passwd > hits.txt 2>&1 work as intended, while grep root /etc/passwd 2>&1 > hits.txt still shows "Permission denied" on the terminal?
quiz.a: In the second form fd 2 is copied from fd 1 while fd 1 still points at the terminal; only afterwards does fd 1 move to hits.txt. Redirections are applied left to right, so order matters.

quiz.q: A script reads a file with for line in $(cat list.txt). Two file names with spaces are read wrongly and a blank line disappears. Explain the cause and the fix.
quiz.a: Unquoted command substitution undergoes word splitting and globbing, so spaces break a name into pieces and empty fields are dropped. Fix: while IFS= read -r line; do ...; done < list.txt, which reads one whole line at a time.

beyond: Not for the exam. Named pipes made with mkfifo, process substitution such as diff <(cmd1) <(cmd2), and extra descriptors opened with exec 3 are the next step; they let one script use several input streams at once. In production, tee in a pipeline keeps a copy of logs while systemd or Docker captures stdout and stderr separately. Search these terms next: process substitution, named pipe, /proc/PID/fd, and shellcheck redirection warnings.
